tagline: Pine forests, river valleys and a highway that changed orchard country
intro: The Billy the Kid Trail crosses grassy plains and pine forest in the Lincoln National Forest. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway at 84 miles, with two hours allowed for driving. New Mexico Tourism presents it as a route through outlaw history, with rivers, orchards and ranchlands linking Lincoln, Ruidoso and Fort Stanton.

The modern road has a story beyond its outlaw name. Federal Aid Project improvements came to the Roswell–Alamogordo road through Ruidoso Downs in the 1920s. At Ruidoso Downs, the road that became US 70 was paved around 1945, improved in 1958 and widened to four lanes in 1981. Realignments near Glencoe left smaller produce stands off the main highway, pushing more families from fruit growing toward ranching.

Begin in Ruidoso, where NM 48 leads north to Capitan. The Rio Bonito passes Fort Stanton and Lincoln before joining the Rio Ruidoso at Hondo. At Hondo, US 380 meets US 70. Follow US 70 west through San Patricio and Glencoe toward Ruidoso Downs. Along the return leg, US 70 follows the Rio Ruidoso valley. The return ends in Ruidoso, a mountain resort town immediately west of Ruidoso Downs.

moments.title: Capitan
moments.text: A bear rescued at Capitan Gap became the living version of a national forest mascot. The village sits between the Capitan and Sacramento Mountains, north of the Lincoln National Forest. High desert mountains, cedar, pinon and juniper surround Capitan. In spring 1950, the badly burned black bear cub was first called Hotfoot Teddy, then renamed Smokey. He went to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., and lived there for 26 years. After his death in November 1976, his remains returned to Capitan for burial at what is now Smokey Bear Historical Park.

moments.title: Fort Stanton
moments.text: Fort Stanton changed from an Army post into a tuberculosis sanatorium. The 1st Dragoon and the 3rd and 8th Infantry Regiments built it in 1855 as a base for military operations against the Mescalero Apaches. The fort’s residents included Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th Cavalry, Kit Carson, Billy the Kid and Pat Garrett. U.S. forces withdrew in 1896; three years later, President William McKinley transferred the property to the Marine Hospital Service. The hospital closed in 1953. Restoration work in 2019 included an original tuberculosis hut and an expansion of the hospital exhibit.

moments.title: Lincoln
moments.text: US 380 is Lincoln’s only street, with the village centered on a one-mile stretch. The Old Lincoln County Courthouse had several lives: store, residence, Masonic Lodge, courthouse and jail. In April 1881, Billy the Kid escaped from custody there after killing the two deputies guarding him. His fame can obscure the larger conflict: the Lincoln County War pitted the Murphy-Dolan and Tunstall-McSween factions against each other for government contracts and local resources. Lincoln’s surviving historic structures include buildings from the late nineteenth century. At the Tunstall Store, original nineteenth-century merchandise is on display.
